Lecture 0-1

Why must process plants cut CO₂ now?

Lecture 0-1 · the plan

From the global budget to a Thai plant's bill

  1. Where emissions come from57 Gt CO₂e a year, mostly energy and industry
  2. The carbon budgetabout four years of today's CO₂ left for 1.5 °C
  3. Neutrality and net zerotwo targets that are not the same
  4. Thailand's commitments and carbon pricethe nationally determined contribution (NDC) and a 200 Thai baht (THB) per tonne tax
  5. Industry's share in Thailandfuel, power and process emissions by sector

From Lecture 12, Decarbonization technologies

57.1 Gt CO₂e in 2023, mostly energy, transport and industry

Power, industry, fuel production and industrial processes together are over half the total — the part chemical engineers design and run.

The carbon budget

Warming follows the total CO₂ ever emitted

Because warming tracks cumulative CO₂, a temperature limit becomes a fixed amount still allowed.

$B$
remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C (Global Carbon Budget 2025)
170 Gt CO₂
$E_0$
this year's global CO₂ emission (2025 projection)
42.2 Gt/yr
$T$
years until the budget is used up
yr
$$B=\int_0^{T}E(t)\,dt$$
$T=\dfrac{B}{E_0}=\dfrac{170}{42.2}=4.0\ \mathrm{yr}$if emissions stay flat
$B=\tfrac12E_0T\ \Rightarrow\ T=\dfrac{2B}{E_0}=8.1\ \mathrm{yr}$if they fall in a straight line to zero

Interactive — spend the budget

How fast must emissions fall?

$$E(t)=E_0e^{-kt},\qquad \int_0^T E\,dt=\dfrac{E_0}{k}\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)$$

$k$ = constant yearly cut (1/yr); the integral is the CO₂ spent by year $T$.

A 2 %/yr cut buys almost nothing; staying inside 170 Gt for ever needs about 25 % less every year.

From Lecture 12, terminology

Carbon neutrality is not net zero

Carbon neutrality

CO₂ emitted is balanced by CO₂ reduced and offset (credits allowed).

Net-zero emission

All greenhouse gases (GHG) cut deeply; only the residue balanced by removal.

Thailand's dates

Carbon neutrality by 2050, net-zero GHG by 2065.

From Lecture 12

Thailand NDC 3.0: 47 % below 2019 by 2035

The NDC is each country's Paris pledge. Thailand's rose from 20–25 % (2020) to 30–40 % (2021), now 47 % below 2019.

From Lecture 12

Carbon now has a price in Thailand

Climate Change Act draft, approved by Cabinet December 2025.

Carbon tax: 200 THB/t CO₂ on six oil products, about 26 % of national emissions.

Also: footprints, an emissions trading scheme (ETS), and the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) on exports.

From Lecture 12 · World Bank, State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2024

Prices today sit far below what 1.5 °C needs

Most prices are under 60 US dollars (USD) per t; the 2030 range for 1.5 °C is USD 226–385/t.

Interactive — what a carbon price does to a product

From THB per tonne CO₂ to THB per tonne product

$$c_p=I\,p_c,\qquad \text{share}=\dfrac{c_p}{P}$$

$I$ t CO₂/t product; $p_c$ carbon price THB/t; $P$ product price THB/t.

carbon cost, THB/t product
share of price
price in USD/t CO₂

At 200 THB/t a carbon tax is a rounding error; at the 1.5 °C range it can take a third of the product's price.

Interactive — Lecture 12 data (fuel and power 2018, process 2019)

Which Thai industries emit, and from what?

■ fuel for electricity
■ fuel burned in processes
■ industrial process (chemistry)

Power generation (96.4 Mt) is left off the scale.

In cement and petrochemicals about half the CO₂ comes from chemistry, not fuel: a fuel switch alone cannot reach zero.

Lecture 0-1 · summary

What section 0-1 settled

  • The 1.5 °C budget is about four years of today's CO₂.
  • Net zero covers all gases and needs removals; neutrality allows offsets.
  • Thailand: −47 % by 2035, neutral by 2050, net zero by 2065; a carbon tax has begun.
  • Half of petrochemical and cement CO₂ is process chemistry, not fuel.

0-2

Lecture 0-2

Which levers exist, and in what order?

Lecture 0-2 · the plan

A toolbox, and the order to open it

  1. Nine abatement approachesfrom circularity to capture and activity reduction
  2. Five pillars, one hierarchysufficiency before efficiency before new supply
  3. How much each pillar deliversthe International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) 2050 shares
  4. Why order mattersefficiency shrinks what electrification must supply
  5. Comparing unlike optionscost per tonne avoided, previewing deck A4

From Lecture 12 · after TheClimateDrive

Nine ways to cut emissions

A process engineer works mostly in rows 2–5, 7 and 8: efficiency, renewable power and heat, new processes, fuel switch and capture.

From Lecture 12

The pyramid: cheapest and surest at the bottom

Nine approaches need an order. Lecture 12 stacks them by cost and certainty.

Avoid the energy, then waste less, then supply the rest cleanly.

IRENA World Energy Transitions Outlook 2023, 1.5 °C scenario

What each pillar delivers by 2050

Renewables 25 %, efficiency 25 %, electrification 19 %, hydrogen 12 %, carbon capture in industry 8 %, removals 11 %.

Half of the cut needs no new molecule: only less energy and cleaner power.

Interactive — apply the pillars in order

From 100 kt of heat CO₂ to the residue

Each step acts on what the previous one left: cheap cuts first make every later, costlier step smaller.

One number for the next example

CO₂ per kWh of steam heat from a gas boiler

$EF_h$
CO₂ per kWh of heat delivered as steam
kg/kWh
$\eta_b$
boiler efficiency, lower-heating-value basis
–
$EF_f$
fuel factor; natural gas 56.1 (IPCC 2006)
kg CO₂/GJ
$EF_h=\dfrac{0.0036\ \mathrm{GJ/kWh}}{\eta_b}\,EF_f$1 kWh is 0.0036 GJ; the boiler loses the rest
$EF_h=\dfrac{0.0036}{0.88}\times56.1=0.2295\ \mathrm{kg/kWh}$boiler 88 % assumed

Example 0.2 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 0.2Electrify now, or integrate first?

Read first

A plant raises 10 MW of process heat as gas-fired steam (boiler 88 %, natural gas 56.1 kg CO₂/GJ) for 8,000 h/yr. It plans to replace all of it with heat pumps of COP 3 driven by on-site solar that yields 1,450 kWh per kWp per year.

  1. Find the heat emission factor.
  2. Find the electricity and solar capacity needed if it electrifies now.
  3. Repeat (b) after first cutting heat demand 20 % by heat integration.
  4. Compare the CO₂ avoided per year.

Example 0.2 · solution

EXAMPLE 0.2Same tonnes, 4 MWp less solar

Previous slide and Lecture 07$EF_h=0.2295\ \mathrm{kg/kWh},\qquad W=Q/\mathrm{COP}$
$W=10/3=3.33\ \mathrm{MW_e};\ \ \dfrac{3333\times8760}{1450}=20.1\ \mathrm{MW_p}$(b) energy basis, no storage
$W=8/3=2.67\ \mathrm{MW_e};\ \ 16.1\ \mathrm{MW_p}$(c) integrate first
$10{,}000\times0.2295\times8000/1000=18{,}360\ \mathrm{t/yr}$(d) both remove all heat CO₂

Integration removes 3,672 t of that with no new power plant at all.

Interactive — Example 0.2 generalised

How much solar does efficiency save?

Example 0.2$\mathrm{MW_p}=\dfrac{Q(1-e)}{\mathrm{COP}}\cdot\dfrac{8760}{Y}$

Every megawatt saved by efficiency is about 2 MWp of solar that never has to be built at COP 3.

Preview of deck A4

One yardstick: THB per tonne avoided

The hierarchy gives the order in principle. Money decides it in practice.

MAC
marginal abatement cost: net yearly cost per tonne avoided
THB/t
$$\mathrm{MAC}=\dfrac{\text{annualised capital}+\Delta\text{operating cost}}{\text{tonnes avoided per year}}$$

Negative MAC: the measure saves money. Efficiency measures usually sit there.

Lecture 0-2 · summary

What section 0-2 settled

  • Open the toolbox in order: sufficiency, efficiency, clean supply, then capture.
  • Half of the 2050 cut is efficiency and renewables (IRENA).
  • Gas steam heat carries about 0.23 kg CO₂/kWh.
  • Efficiency first shrinks the new supply; rank options by THB per tonne.

0-3

Lecture 0-3

What does this mean for one process plant?

Lecture 0-3 · the plan

From the policy to the plant

  1. Where a plant's energy money goesenergy is 90–95 % of utility cost
  2. Efficiency multiplies along the chainboiler × turbine × wires × motor × pump
  3. How a chemical company plans itScopes 1, 2, 3 and a dated target (BASF)
  4. Which lever moves which scopeelectrified steam and green power
  5. The map of this serieswhich deck answers which loss, with C-201 as a preview

Utilities in a petrochemical plant

Energy is 90–95 % of the utility bill

Policy sets the target; a plant meets it one kilowatt at a time.

Steam, electricity and fuel drive every unit; they are the utility cost.

$\eta$
efficiency: useful energy output over total energy input
–
$$\eta=\dfrac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}$$

Example: a motor drawing 100 W that delivers 90 W of shaft power is 90 % efficient.

Example 0.3 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 0.3The efficiency chain

Read first

A power boiler (90 %) raises steam for a turbo generator (40 %); the power is transmitted to the plant (90 %).

  1. Find the overall system efficiency.
  2. The power then drives a 90 % motor and a 70 % pump. How many kW of fuel are burned per kW of hydraulic power delivered to the fluid?

Example 0.3 · solution

EXAMPLE 0.3Five kW of fuel for one kW at the fluid

Previous slides$\eta=\dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{input}},\qquad \eta_{overall}=\textstyle\prod_i\eta_i$
$\eta_{1-3}=0.90\times0.40\times0.90=0.324$(a) each stage passes on its share
$\eta_{1-5}=0.324\times0.90\times0.70=0.204$add motor and pump
$1/0.204=4.9\ \mathrm{kW\ fuel\ per\ kW\ hydraulic}$(b)

A kW saved at the pump saves almost 5 kW of fuel at the boiler.

Interactive — fix the weakest link

Where does the fuel go?

Chain efficiency $\eta_{overall}=\prod_i\eta_i$ (Example 0.3).

Five points on the 40 % turbine save twice the fuel of five points on the 90 % boiler: improve the weakest link first.

TNChE 2024: "Role of chemical industry in driving decarbonization" (BASF)

Most of a chemical company's footprint is outside its fence

Targets: −25 % Scope 1 + 2 by 2030 against 2018, net zero by 2050; −16 % reached by 2022.

Main levers named: renewable power, power-to-steam (e-boilers, heat pumps, e-drives), an electric steam-cracker furnace.

Interactive — an illustrative plant

Electrifying steam moves CO₂ between scopes

Section 0-2$\dot E_{el}=\dfrac{Q}{\mathrm{COP}}EF_g$

Plant: Scope 1 = 60 kt (all steam fuel), Scope 2 = 40 kt, grid 0.475, $EF_h$ 0.2295.

An e-boiler on today's grid doubles the steam's CO₂ and only moves it to Scope 2: electrify with a heat pump, or with green power.

Lecture 0-3 · summary

What section 0-3 settled

  • Energy is 90–95 % of a petrochemical plant's utility cost.
  • Efficiencies multiply: 1 kW at the pump can cost 5 kW of fuel.
  • Most of a chemical company's footprint is Scope 3; its own 1 + 2 is what engineers move.
  • Electrifying heat helps only with a heat pump or green power.

Problem 0.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 0.1A plant's carbon bill

Read first

A plant produces 200,000 t/yr of product and consuming 3,500 × 10⁶ megajoules (MJ) per year of energy. Treat all of that energy as natural-gas equivalent at 56.1 kg CO₂/GJ.

  1. Find the energy intensity (MJ/t) and the CO₂ intensity (t CO₂/t product).
  2. Find the yearly carbon cost at Thailand's 200 THB/t and at USD 100/t (33.5 THB/USD).
GivenValue
Production200,000 t/yr
Energy3,500 × 10⁶ MJ/yr
Fuel factor56.1 kg CO₂/GJ
Carbon prices200 THB/t; USD 100/t

Problem 0.1 · solution

PROBLEM 0.139 million THB today, 658 million at USD 100

Section 0-1$c_p=I\,p_c$
$3500\times10^6/200{,}000=17{,}500\ \mathrm{MJ/t}$(a) energy intensity
$3.5\times10^6\ \mathrm{GJ}\times56.1=196{,}350\ \mathrm{t\,CO_2/yr};\ I=0.98$(a) per tonne of product
$196{,}350\times200=39.3\ \mathrm{MTHB/yr}$(b) Thai tax rate
$196{,}350\times100\times33.5=658\ \mathrm{MTHB/yr}$(b) 17 times more

Problem 0.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 0.2A slow decline

Read first

World CO₂ emissions are 42.2 Gt/yr and the remaining 1.5 °C budget is 170 Gt. (a) If emissions fall 2 % per year, continuously, when is the budget spent? (b) What constant yearly cut would keep all future emissions inside the budget?

Section 0-1, recalled$\int_0^T E_0e^{-kt}\,dt=\dfrac{E_0}{k}\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)$

Problem 0.2 · solution

PROBLEM 0.2Two percent a year buys two months

Section 0-1$B=\dfrac{E_0}{k}\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)$
$T=-\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\!\left(1-\dfrac{kB}{E_0}\right)$solve for $T$
$T=-\dfrac{1}{0.02}\ln\!\left(1-\dfrac{0.02\times170}{42.2}\right)=4.2\ \mathrm{yr}$(a) versus 4.0 when flat
$\dfrac{E_0}{k}\le B\Rightarrow k\ge\dfrac{42.2}{170}=0.25\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$(b) about 25 % less every year

Problem 0.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 0.3A sector efficiency target

Read first

Thailand's petrochemical & refinery sector emits 25,126,965 t CO₂e (Example 0.1 table). A programme of heat recovery cuts the fuel burned in processes by 30 %. (a) By how much does the sector total fall? (b) Why can no fuel measure reach the remaining 46.8 %?

Sourcet CO₂e
Fuel for electricity2,802,402
Fuel in processes10,568,273
Industrial processes11,756,290

Problem 0.3 · solution

PROBLEM 0.3A 30 % fuel cut is a 12.6 % sector cut

Example 0.1$\Delta E=f\,E_{fuel},\qquad \text{share}=\Delta E/E_{total}$
$0.30\times10{,}568{,}273=3{,}170{,}482\ \mathrm{t}$(a) only the fuel-in-process row
$3{,}170{,}482/25{,}126{,}965=12.6\,\%$(a) share of the sector

(b) Process emissions come from the chemistry itself — CO₂ released by the reaction or by burning off-gas the process makes. Only new routes, new feedstocks or capture reach them.

Before you leave

Key Takeaways

1

Treat the budget as urgent: about four years of today's CO₂ remain for 1.5 °C.

2

Know Thailand's dates: −47 % by 2035, neutral 2050, net zero 2065.

3

Attack in order: sufficiency, efficiency, clean supply, capture.

4

Fix the weakest link: efficiencies multiply along the chain.

5

Electrify heat with a heat pump or green power, never a gas-grid e-boiler.
